planting.note: Set out rhizome crown divisions around last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Morado is a darker-skinned Andean strain and is otherwise grown exactly like standard yacon, dying back at first fall frost while its roots and crowns overwinter in the ground in zones 7-9 under mulch.

directions: Morado is a traditional Andean strain of yacon distinguished from the common tan-skinned type by its deep reddish-purple tuber skin and correspondingly purple-flushed stem bases, though the crisp, juicy, pear-like flesh inside remains cream to pale yellow. Grow it exactly as standard yacon: propagate only from the knobby rhizome crowns at the base of last season's stalks (never from the large storage roots, which lack buds and will not sprout), and give it a long, frost-free season of at least five to six months to bulk up its tubers. Many growers who maintain both types report Morado yields slightly smaller but more numerous roots than pale-skinned strains, with a similar sweet, watery crunch that intensifies after a week or two of post-harvest curing in a warm, sunny spot. Because it is an old landrace rather than a registered cultivar, plant vigor and skin color can vary somewhat between sources.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) -- Andean Roots and Tubers

common_name: Lily White Sea Kale (Vigorous Seed-Raised Forcing Strain)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring in deep, sandy, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Lily White is a selected seed strain bred for uniform germination and unusually pale, tender forced shoots, and like the species it needs two full growing seasons before its first light harvest.

directions: Lily White is a named UK seed strain of sea kale selected over generations for producing especially pale, blanch-white forced shoots with minimal bitterness, along with more reliably true germination from seed than typical wild-collected sea kale seed. It forms the same billowing mounds of crinkled, blue-gray, cabbage-like leaves and honey-scented white summer flowers as the species, and is grown identically: choose a permanent bed for its long taproot, let plants establish for two to three years, then cover dormant crowns with a forcing pot in late winter to produce sweet, nutty, asparagus-textured shoots in early spring. Because plants are deep-rooted and drought-tolerant once established, they perform especially well in coastal gardens and sandy, low-fertility soils where few other vegetables thrive.

common_name: Boston Red Sunchoke (Heirloom Red-Skinned Jerusalem Artichoke)

planting.note: Plant tuber pieces 4-6 inches deep around last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; Boston Red is an old New England heirloom grown for its deep red-skinned, moderately knobby tubers and should be sited in a permanent, contained bed since it spreads readily from any tuber left behind.

directions: Boston Red is a long-grown New England heirloom sunchoke selected for its striking maroon-red tuber skin, which contrasts sharply with the white flesh beneath and makes it a favorite of seed savers maintaining regionally distinct strains. Like other Jerusalem artichokes it grows into a coarse, sunflower-like stand 6-10 feet tall, topped with small yellow flowers in late summer, and tolerates poor soil and neglect once established. Dig tubers after the tops are killed by frost and continue harvesting through winter and into early spring as needed, leaving some tubers in the ground each year to regenerate the patch. Its flavor is the same nutty, sweet-earthy inulin-rich profile typical of the species, and it sweetens further after tubers experience a hard freeze.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension -- Jerusalem Artichoke
